subject: astronomy

moments.title: New Horizons flies past Pluto
moments.body: Launched in 2006, New Horizons reaches Pluto on 14 July 2015 — and finds a geologically active world: nitrogen ice glaciers, water-ice mountains, a heart-shaped plain (Tombaugh Regio). At Pluto's distance, sunlight is ~1/1000 of Earth's. New Horizons later flies past Arrokoth (1 January 2019), a binary contact object in the Kuiper Belt.
moments.takeaway: Pluto turned out to be one of the most surprising worlds in the solar system. Smaller worlds are not necessarily dead worlds.

moments.title: Pluto reclassified
moments.body: On 24 August 2006, the IAU defines 'planet' such that Pluto becomes a 'dwarf planet'. The decision is controversial. Discoverer Clyde Tombaugh's widow protests. New Horizons launches months earlier — to a planet that becomes a dwarf planet en route.
moments.takeaway: Categories in science are conventions. Pluto did not change; the definition did.

now.title: Outer solar system today
now.body: The Kuiper Belt contains ~100,000 objects >100 km diameter. Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Sedna are major dwarf planets. The Vera Rubin Observatory (2025-) will discover thousands more. A hypothetical 'Planet Nine' (~6 Earth masses, ~400-800 AU) may explain orbital clustering of distant objects.
now.open_questions: Does Planet Nine exist? Surveys are searching.

reflection: When New Horizons launched (2006), Pluto was a planet. When it arrived (2015), it was a dwarf planet. The mission's principal investigator Alan Stern remains a vocal critic of the 2006 reclassification.
